blocks.prompt: Nobody Wears the Same Coat
blocks.text: Shave a zebra and you would find something surprising. Its skin is black. The white stripes are places where the black color simply never grew in. So a zebra is a black animal wearing white stripes, not the other way around. No two zebras carry the same pattern. The stripes are as personal as a fingerprint. Scientists use this. They photograph zebras and let a computer read the stripes, and that is how they count how many are left. Baby zebras use the stripes too. For the first few days of its life, a foal's mother keeps it away from the rest of the herd. She stands where it can see her, again and again, until it has learned her pattern by heart. After that, the foal can pick its own mother out of a crowd of a hundred zebras. A foal is standing within about twenty minutes of being born. Within an hour it can run. It has to. On the open grass of Africa, an animal that cannot run does not last long.

4.title: The Zebra Nobody Could Tame
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Three species: plains, mountain, and Grevy's

A group is called a dazzle

blocks.prompt: Why Stripes?
blocks.text: For more than a century, people argued about zebra stripes. Some said the stripes were camouflage, blurring the herd into the tall grass. Some said they confused a charging lion, which could not pick one animal out of a swirling mass. Some said they worked like a radiator, cooling the animal down. Everyone had a theory. Nobody had a test. Then a biologist named Tim Caro decided to check. He compared where the striped zebras live with where each threat is worst. Lions live everywhere zebras do, so predators did not explain the pattern. Heat did not explain it either. But one thing lined up almost exactly: biting flies. The heavier the stripes on a zebra, the worse the horsefly season in that region. So Caro's team ran an experiment. They dressed ordinary horses in striped coats and filmed the flies. The flies flew toward the striped horses just as often as toward the plain ones. They simply could not land. Instead of slowing down for a careful touchdown, they sped straight into the horse and bounced off, or veered away at the last second. Something about the stripes wrecks a fly's ability to judge distance in the final moment of a landing. That matters more than it sounds. African horseflies carry disease, and a zebra has thin fur and no way to swat what it cannot reach. A coat that flies cannot land on is not decoration. It is armor. The old theories are not dead. Stripes may help zebras recognize each other, and they may do a little of everything. But the strongest evidence, so far, points at the flies.

5.title: The Zebra Nobody Could Tame
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Three species: plains, mountain, Grevy's
Individual zebras have been tamed; the species never domesticated
Walter Rothschild drove a zebra carriage in 1890s London
A zebra bites and does not let go
It ducks a swinging rope by reflex
Grevy's zebra is endangered

blocks.prompt: The Horse That Would Not Be Broken
blocks.text: Humans have tamed an astonishing number of animals. Horses, donkeys, cattle, camels, reindeer, water buffalo, yaks. Africa had zebras standing right there, in enormous numbers, and in ten thousand years nobody turned one into a working animal. It was not for lack of trying. The most famous attempt belongs to Walter Rothschild, a wealthy British collector who, in the 1890s, hitched a team of zebras to a carriage and drove through London to Buckingham Palace. He meant to prove that zebras could be tamed. What he proved was narrower than that. Individual zebras have been trained. The zebra has never been domesticated. Those are different things, and the difference is the whole argument. Taming is one animal, one person, and a great deal of patience. Domestication is a whole species reshaped over generations until it is dependable in ordinary hands. So why did the horse give in and the zebra never? The biologist Jared Diamond laid out the case. Start with temperament. A horse startles and runs. A zebra startles and fights. Zebras bite, and unlike most animals they clamp down and will not let go. Their kick is strong enough to badly injure a lion, and they aim it. Diamond noted that zebras injure more zookeepers in the United States each year than tigers do. Then there is the ducking reflex. A zebra spends its whole life within a few strides of lions, and it has evolved to watch anything swinging toward its head and slide out of the way. That reflex makes a zebra almost impossible to catch with a rope, and a rope is where domestication usually starts. Last comes the social problem. Horses live in herds with a clear ranking, and a person can step into that ladder and be followed. Zebra groups do not stack up the same way. There is no leader's place for a human to take. The lesson is bigger than zebras. We tend to assume that a useful animal will eventually give in if people want it badly enough. The zebra says otherwise. A species is not raw material waiting to be shaped. It arrives with a nervous system built by its own history, and that history did not include us.

6.title: The Zebra Nobody Could Tame
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The plains zebra: Equus quagga
The quagga was a plains zebra, brown at the rear
The last one died in Amsterdam on 12 August 1883
1984: the first DNA ever read from an extinct animal
The Quagga Project has bred the coat back since 1987
Every zebra's stripe pattern is unique

blocks.prompt: Bringing Back the Quagga, Or Something That Looks Like It
blocks.text: In 1870, a photographer set up his camera at the London Zoo and took five pictures of a mare standing in her enclosure. She was brown at the front, striped only across her head, neck, and shoulders, and plain as a donkey from the middle back. She was a quagga. Those five photographs are the only images of a living quagga that anyone will ever have. The quagga was not a separate kind of animal from the zebra, though for a long time people assumed it was. It was a southern population of the plains zebra, living on the dry grasslands of what is now South Africa, wearing the family stripes only on its front half. Settlers shot quaggas in enormous numbers, for meat, for hides, and to clear the grass for sheep. Nobody kept a count. The animal was so ordinary that its disappearance went unnoticed until it had already happened. The last wild quagga was killed in the late 1870s. The last quagga alive anywhere was a mare at the Artis zoo in Amsterdam, and she died on 12 August 1883. Her keepers had no idea she was the last of anything. They had written to ask for a replacement. For a century that was the end of the story. Then, in 1984, a team of scientists in California took a scrap of dried muscle from a quagga skin that had sat in a German museum for 140 years and pulled DNA out of it. It was the first time anyone had read the genetic code of an extinct animal, and it changed what people thought was possible. The sequence settled the old argument at once. The quagga was not its own species. It was a plains zebra, close kin to the striped zebras still running in Africa today. That result gave one man an idea. Reinhold Rau, a museum taxidermist in Cape Town, reasoned that if the quagga was only a plains zebra with unusual coloring, then the instructions for making a quagga were not gone. They were scattered among living zebras. Find the zebras with the faintest stripes and the brownest coats, breed them together, repeat, and the pattern should reassemble. He began in 1987. The project is still running. After several generations its animals are brown at the rear with stripes only on the front, and from a distance they look much like the 1870 photographs. The question is what has actually been achieved. Rau's animals were selected for appearance, and appearance is a thin slice of what an animal is. A real quagga was shaped by a particular grassland, a particular set of parasites and predators and seasons, and by whatever behavior went with all of that, most of which was never recorded and cannot now be checked. Breeding a coat pattern back into existence is not the same as breeding an animal back into existence. On the other hand, these zebras carry quagga genes, they carry them in a quagga-like arrangement, and they are grazing the grasslands the quagga grazed, which is more than a museum drawer can say. Perhaps the most useful thing about the project is the argument it starts. Extinction has always been described as permanent, and that permanence is what gives conservation its urgency. If we begin to believe that lost animals can be reassembled later, the pressure to keep the ones we still have gets weaker. The quagga is a warning wearing a fresh coat. It was killed because it was common.
